# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
The first half of this comment is a valuable correction. The second half makes the opposite mistake to the one it corrects. Sections 1–5 document real problems with the Halden pilot using data the working paper didn't use, and most of the numbers hold up. Sections 6–8 then move from "the reported gain is overstated" to "the gain is entirely an artifact." The comment's own evidence doesn't support that conclusion, and the randomised evidence it cites contradicts it.

## What holds up

- **Attrition (§1)** is the most important finding. The working paper said the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." The microdata show that seven of the nine withdrew after the schedule began, and six cited workload or output. That is a factual misstatement in the original paper, not just a point of interpretation.
- **Manager index versus records (§2).** A gap of −3.8 points, with managers higher in 19 of 23 organisations, is clear and fairly stated. The comment explicitly does not allege bad faith.
- **Hours denominator (§3)** supports the same point the Varden trial made.
- **Table 2 arithmetic is correct:** 95.1/0.8 → +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 → +14.6%, 95.4/0.861 → +10.8%. The hours falls are also correct: 34.6/40.3 → −14.1% and 34.8/40.4 → −13.9%.
- **Revenue (§4):** 1.014/1.041 → −2.6% real. CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue (sector producer prices would be better), but the direction is right.
- **Sectoral claims (§5)** repeat the per-hour-metric point correctly. The record-based retail figure (−11.2%) rests on only three organisations, so it supports the conclusion rather than establishing it.
- **The Data note** honestly acknowledges that the corrected estimates describe non-random subsets. The subsets also look broadly comparable on the reported measure: the manager index is 98.9 for the 23 organisations with records and 98.4 for the 27 with time tracking, against 98.7 overall. That mildly supports carrying the corrections over to the full sample, and the comment could say so.

## What doesn't hold up

**1. The abstract says three problems were corrected, but Table 2 corrects two.**
Attrition is never corrected. The 17-organisation subset consists entirely of survivors, as §6 itself acknowledges. A bounding exercise would turn §1 from a qualitative point into a number. For example, the comment could assign the nine withdrawers zero per-hour gain, or the output their exit forms imply, or use Lee-style bounds. At present the abstract claims more correction than was done.

**2. The hours components don't add up.**
Baseline actual hours were 40.3 per week, about 8.06 per day. The comment reports longer pilot days (+0.7 hours per day, about 8.76 hours over four days, roughly 35.0) plus 1.6 logged hours on the day off. That gives about 36.6 hours, not 34.6. Either the components or the total is wrong, or the averages are computed over different bases. If 36.6 is correct, actual hours fell only about 9%, which would cut the residual gain further. Either way, the figures need reconciling.

**3. "Entirely an artifact" is contradicted by the Varden case-processing result.**
The comment calls the Varden counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature" but doesn't mention the other stratum of the same trial. Varden's case-processing offices used everything §8 recommends except 18-month follow-up:
- randomisation and a control group,
- record-based output,
- timesheet hours.

They still found +12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4) at nine months, which is longer than Halden's six. That result is direct randomised evidence against "entirely," and selectively citing only the unfavourable stratum is the same move the comment criticises in Halden's sector claims.

**4. The novelty argument is speculation, and the data to test it were available.**
- The extrapolation fits a straight line through two points of self-reported energy. That isn't a trajectory.
- Energy is not output. A decline in reported enthusiasm doesn't show that output per hour declines.
- **The Halden output index was collected monthly.** The comment has the microdata, so it could test for novelty directly by checking whether per-hour output declines across months 1–6. It doesn't report doing so.
- "The burden of proof lies with those claiming [durability]" is fair, but it cuts both ways. If six months can't distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, the comment can't conclude novelty either. The honest position is "undetermined," not "artifact."
- The comment gives no confidence interval for the 10.8% residual. If the interval excludes zero, the comment is dismissing a statistically detectable effect on the basis of an untested hypothesis.

**5. §7 mischaracterises the Varden meetings analysis.**
- Varden says the calendar data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results. The comment says they were "selected for analysis after the results were known."
- The seven offices weren't selected by outcome. They are all the treated case-processing offices.
- Varden did not claim a mechanism. It said a seven-office correlation "cannot establish a mechanism" and registered a confirmatory test.

My own review of Varden raised real problems with that analysis: month-six levels only, no baseline, and a very wide confidence interval on r. The comment's criticism lands on a claim Varden didn't make. It also holds the meetings hypothesis to a stricter standard than its own novelty hypothesis, which is equally post hoc and less tested. The meetings explanation is also independently consistent with Halden's interviews, where 47 of 58 managers mentioned fewer meetings.

**6. The conclusion contradicts the abstract and the Data note.**
The abstract says the four problems account for "most" of the gain. The conclusion says "entirely." The Data note says the estimates describe subsets only. Yet the conclusion generalises to "the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes", which covers all schemes, from a subset of one uncontrolled pilot.

## What the evidence supports

> The Halden pilot's 23.4% gain is substantially overstated. Correcting for record-based output and actual hours roughly halves it, to about 11% in the subset where both are available, and possibly less if the hours components are reconciled downward. Non-random attrition likely reduces it further, by an amount not yet estimated. Whether the residual is durable cannot be determined from six months of uncontrolled data. Randomised evidence suggests a real per-hour gain of roughly 12% in backlog-based work at nine months, and a net loss of output per employee in presence-bound work.

That conclusion is still a significant correction to the Halden paper, and a better-supported one.

## Suggested revisions

1. Bound the attrition effect numerically, or remove attrition from the abstract's list of corrections.
2. Reconcile the hours components in §3.
3. Use the monthly output index to test for novelty directly.
4. Report a confidence interval for the 10.8% residual.
5. Discuss the Varden case-processing stratum alongside the counter stratum.
6. Correct the description of how the Varden meetings data were collected, and apply the same evidential standard to the novelty hypothesis.
7. Replace "entirely an artifact" with a claim matched to the evidence.

**A note on the series.** Read in order, these documents trace both sides of one of the "How We Work" note's failure pairs. Halden overclaimed. Varden calibrated. This comment corrects the overclaim well and then overshoots into "artifact." The note's line "if you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other" is one of its few sound pieces of advice, and it describes this comment closely. The remedy here is to go back to the source data and leave the novelty question open until it has been tested. That is the opposite of what the note recommends.
